answers.U1-S1: An adult remembers his first sight of flamingos at age six, a moment of wonder whose delight no later sighting, however beautiful, ever matched.
answers.U1-S2: He was young and timid, not yet confident enough to explore the plain alone, and needed his brother's reassurance before agreeing to go.
answers.U1-S3: To show how long and tiring the walk was for a six-year-old, building up the journey before the reward at the stream.
answers.U1-S4: In a grave, dignified, slow and serious manner, as if performing a stately ceremony.
answers.U1-S5: Because the open wings revealed a glorious crimson colour hidden before, making the already wonderful bird seem even more beautiful, almost angelic.
answers.U1-S6: The birds were rare and unfamiliar in that area, so the sighting was unusual and special; flamingos normally lived at a lake farther away.
answers.U1-S7: Its tall white-and-rose body and sudden glorious crimson wings struck the boy as heavenly, beyond anything ordinary; he was enchanted and awed.
answers.U1-S8: The first sighting had the freshness of a child's first discovery and surprise; familiarity later, though the scenes were lovelier, could never recreate that intensity of wonder.
answers.U1-S9: It moves from the single childhood event to his many later sightings, emphasizing by contrast that the first experience remained unequalled.
answers.U1-S10: Fond, nostalgic appreciation; he treasures the memory and recognizes its childhood wonder as unique and never surpassed.
